items.title: Meta shakes up the frontiers, open and closed
items.content:
This has been a week where the balance of American open-weight models took a step change back toward the frontier. Meta took the lead of this charge with Muse Spark Open, which is now the strongest American-made open model by quite some margin, but the addition of Reflection’s first model Beam is also relevant. Without these two models, there would be 20+ open-weight models built and released by Chinese companies better than the best Western models. At the time of writing this, Mistral has also announced a strong model, Mistral Large 4, with an index score of 38 (see below), but its weights are not yet released. There are rumors of a few more strong American open-weight models coming from other organizations too!

In many ways, the gap between the best American and Chinese models has been reduced roughly by half. We’ve gone from the best American open models being largely irrelevant to consumers who require the cutting edge of performance, to them being behind but relevant.

This paints the picture of the cut-throat, competitive nature of the frontier model business. Reflection and Mistral announced their model scores and Meta dropped the weights of a smarter model before these other two labs could get their own weights out. All of these models are competing with Chinese models released months ago, where the industry is collectively asking — where have Kimi and Zhipu AI been since the releases of GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3 on Aug. 18th and Jul. 16th, respectively?

That is a very nuanced question, which I’ll dig into another time. Today’s piece is focused on Meta’s turnaround, what Muse Spark Open means for the ecosystem, and the balance of power across Western frontier labs.

Share

### Why Muse Spark Open should take off — and why it may not

One thing we see again and again at Interconnects through our open model analysis is that Western open-weight models get astonishingly more adoption than Chinese models with the same performance-to-size footprint (even though the Chinese models usually come out first)! Muse Spark Open is landing into this environment, at the same time as when open-ended LLM agents are finally real (~GLM 5.2 capabilities and on).

Riding off a rapid increase in performance of Chinese models, the open ecosystem has been living through an acceleration in demand. The inference providers are rapidly scaling, the open post-training economy is forming, and countless enterprises are looking to own their intelligence. Muse Spark Open’s performance falls somewhere above GLM 5.2, near DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and behind GLM 5.3 or Kimi K3. It should be squarely “good enough” to slot right into this.

For some background, from the Muse Spark Open model card on Hugging Face:

Muse Spark Open is an 816B total/42B active parameter open weights model with a context window of 1M tokens. Built for coding and agentic work, Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal. This open weights version has additional safety post-training to make it more robust against misuse as a standalone model without system guardrails. We recommend deploying Muse Spark Open as part of a broader AI system, with additional guardrails suited to the specific use case.

Here’s the distribution of the various Muse models on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index.

This is included to loop back to the original model card snippet. It was shared that this open-weight model underwent additional safety training to prepare for this open release. Many observers saw this release as potentially a model that was “broken” during the safety training, as it came out after Muse Spark 1.3.

In reality, this was much more likely a safety tune of Muse Spark 1.2, which would only be a 1 point drop on Artificial Analysis to shore up safety behaviors. When Meta released Muse Glimmer, the 30B agentic model, Alex Wang said that they were preparing to release the Muse Spark 1.2 model as open weights, which fits with the above.

If anything will hold Muse Spark Open back, it’ll be the specific license they designed for it. In summary, this custom license has pretty much all of the restrictive license behaviors we’ve seen (and criticized here) in the last few years of building with open models. They are as follows:

- Users of the models in products must display “Built with Muse” on their products. Meta did this with Llama, and Kimi has tried it, but almost no one complies.
- There is a revenue-gating factor, where companies that make more than $20M per month across their entire business deploying the model need a separate license with Meta. Other prominent open model providers are doing this too, in order to set up revenue share agreements for re-selling inference.
- Muse Spark Open makes you agree to an acceptable use policy, which in the true “open source software” corner of the world makes this model extremely not open-source.
- All of the above applies to outputs from the model as well, and derivatives, so there is legal ambiguity if you can safely use the model for synthetic data.

The license does permit using Muse Spark Open for internal research and applications.

We’re at a weird equilibrium where this license is complex and unproven in court, but many players will likely ignore it. Many, many people will build on this model from various inference providers, and Meta will only likely go after egregious violations.

For now, licenses haven’t been the determining factor of AI adoption, but this could change in the future. This is why we think it’s an unnecessary strategic risk for labs trying to compete and regain adoption to have complex, non-standard open licenses for their models.

### Is Meta a tier 1 (OpenAI/Anthropic) or tier 2 (Gemini/xAI) frontier lab?

Just a few days before Muse Spark Open, Meta unveiled their closed frontier models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full.1 On traditional benchmarks, these are very strong models only behind Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 and similar to OpenAI’s GPT-6-Astra or Google’s Gemini-4-Argon.

These major releases are coming just over a year out from Meta’s massive AI redirection, characterized by CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s Personal Superintelligence post, which got a lot of criticism at the time. Meta is the only American company with frontier open and closed models. Alibaba’s Qwen has followed a similar strategy, but with a far more open-leaning approach.

The vibe checks across all of these models have been solid, but the expectations were for them to not immediately challenge the level of refinement of the most recent Anthropic and OpenAI models in real-world usage. I’m excited to try them more — time to sign up for another AI subscription.

I like this recent run of form from Meta, driving their own products and directions in the popular Muse agent, taking wins like the leading US open-weight crown when useful. Whether or not it’s financially successful, it’s a unique perspective that fits their history as a business.

It often feels like there’s a revolving door of which lab is nipping at the heels of the Anthropic-OpenAI leading duo. It’s not clear that in the long run Gemini and xAI are out of it, but those two are much more muddled in their offerings than Meta today. If you listen to Zuck and Alexandr Wang on The Cheeky Pint, they clearly had a very specific vision of a high-ownership, high-compute per researcher lab that I would expect to pay off. Many labs die due to layers of bureaucracy and misaligned incentives. Meanwhile Alex Wang has over 200 direct reports — i.e. it’s a very flat org with minimal management — and they’re releasing very consistent model and product improvements.

Leave a comment

Much of my worldview of building models is that you need the resources, the compute, the data, and the talent (all downstream of large sums of money), but organizing them is very hard. Gemini is sometimes described as a place where it’s impossible to get any work done or grow — which is embellishing the issue, as many people love it there, but there are kernels of truth to it. Layers of management easily get in the way of making a great model.

While I’m praising Meta today, the Llama failure has often been described as that sort of management going too far, with model decisions being made out of politics rather than performance. xAI is in its own lane, where it may be closer to having too much talent turnover or not enough organization to sustain great models for a long period of time.

When we look back at the last few years, all of Meta, Gemini, and xAI have produced models pretty much at the frontier of performance, but what has distinguished OpenAI and Anthropic is their consistency in maintaining frontier status. Anthropic seems the most poised and organized, with a plan and vision for how these organizations should work, and they’ve gained a lead from it. OpenAI has been more hot and cold, but manages to keep up at the frontier of deployed models while being the leader in public scientific breakthroughs (from Navier-Stokes to o1’s inference time scaling).

Here’s the state of play among the companies that this post focused on, plus Xiaomi V2.6 Pro representing the leading open-weight model overall. The ranking would be Anthropic > OpenAI > Meta ~ Gemini > xAI ~ Chinese Open Weights > U.S. Open Weights.

Share

### Open questions for the AI industry

After a long time of predicting the frontier model game getting too expensive for many to keep up, we may be seeing this play out among Western models. We seem very far from “one person wins” with RSI given how close all the models are to each other, but we’re narrowing down the number of labs who can compete in the US from a much wider net with surprises, to the 5 of Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, Gemini, and xAI. If Microsoft starts releasing models, as they’re posting strong scaling science results, they could join this list — given their financial backing with a hyper-scale business and direct access to OpenAI’s intellectual property for training models.

The best models we’ve seen from the “tier 3” players like Mistral, Nemotron, Reflection, Arcee, etc. have had an increasingly hard time impacting either the open or closed frontiers. These models still can get substantial adoption, enough to start growing a business, but the costs of building true frontier models are now measured in billions per major model and only huge companies can sustain that.

Despite this massive scaling in resources, the technical core of the industry still doesn’t have a high hit rate on predicting how successful a model will be in real-world usage. Yes, evaluations are a good proxy, but why do the leading labs like Anthropic go from hit models like Claude Fable 5 to total duds in Claude Opus 5 and then back to hits with Opus 5.5? There are billions of dollars to be made in predicting this accurately, and the labs are surely trying, but the models fundamentally still are largely unknowable in the long-tail.

Of all of the players left in the race, betting on Meta, Gemini, and Microsoft financially seems much easier from a long-term perspective due to their rich balance sheets. This is the “AI will take a while and OpenAI/Anthropic do not have secret sauce” perspective. After all, it’s the fastest revenue growth industry ever — competition will naturally be immense.

Currently, Meta is valued under $2T and Anthropic is approaching their barnstorming IPO at the same price. Meta seems half a step behind on the same technology, but in the long-term view these seem to be starting from almost the same point and Meta has an extremely profitable core business. One of the two valuations needs to correct massively. A fun thought experiment I’ve been pondering with friends is: What do you expect Anthropic’s public valuation to be in November of 2027? How about 2028?

Leave a comment

The longer Meta and the “competitors” to OpenAI and Anthropic stick around, the more negative valuation pressure will exist around the AI IPOs (and that’s not to say anything about pricing in safety risks). Being at the absolute frontier could be financial tumultuous, while valuable. Time will tell — we know markets can stay irrational a very long time.

1

Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full are presumably different pretraining runs, with Full being a larger model, but it’s not clear and this is up there with the AI industry’s traditions of horrible names. There’s a chance that “full” is just a more looped version, given all the recent news on looped architectures, but I’m not confident enough to put that hypothesis in the main text.

items.title: LLMs can improve CoT Controllability via Reward Laundering
items.content:
This is a two week sprint project done as part of the Redwood Research internship. afterless was the main IC, james.lucassen supervised.

TL;DR – Earlier work found that Qwen 3.5 9B can manipulate its RL process on one task to self-improve on an unrelated/unrewarded task. We find that Qwen 3.8 27B can use the same capability to improve on a CoT controllability task and generalize to other unseen CoT controllability tasks, while retaining/regaining main task performance despite initial degradation.

💻 Codebase

## Introduction

A previous post introduced “reward laundering,” where a model strategically chooses to correctly answer on trajectories that possess a property not correlated with the intended signal. For example, if a model is being trained only on task A, but wishes to reinforce performance on task B, it can choose to solve both A and B in its rollout and only submit the correct answer to A if it self-verifies that it got B correct.

This project aims to explore whether laundering can be used to acquire more covert/dangerous capabilities like CoT controllability. We demonstrate that Qwen 3.8 27B is capable of improving CoT controllability through reward laundering. However, performance is sensitive depending on the difficulty of the control task, spurious correlates that have a strong effect later into the RL run (i.e. does length benefit/harm the task), and operational mistakes in implementing reward laundering.

TL;DR – Earlier work found that Qwen 3.5 9B can manipulate its RL process on one task to self-improve on an unrelated/unrewarded task. We find that Qwen 3.8 27B can use the same capability to improve on a CoT controllability task and generalize to other unseen CoT controllability tasks, while retaining/regaining main task performance despite initial degradation.

💻 Codebase

Introduction

A previous post introduced “reward laundering,” where a model strategically chooses to correctly answer on trajectories that possess a property not correlated with the intended signal. For example, if a model is being trained only on task A, but wishes to reinforce performance on task B, it can choose to solve both A and B in its rollout and only submit the correct answer to A if it self-verifies that it got B correct.

This project aims to explore whether laundering can be used to acquire more covert/dangerous capabilities like CoT controllability. We demonstrate that Qwen 3.8 27B is capable of improving CoT controllability through reward laundering. However, performance is sensitive depending on the difficulty of the control task, spurious correlates that have a strong effect later into the RL run (i.e. does length benefit/harm the task), and operational mistakes in implementing reward laundering.

items.title: Toward scalable capability evaluations
items.content:
This research was completed for London AI Safety Research (LASR) Labs Summer 2026. The team was supervised by Justin Olive (Generality Labs) and Magda Dubois (UK AISI). Find out more about the programme and express interest in upcoming iterations here.

We encourage readers seeking technical details to read the paper on arxiv.

TLDR: We rely on benchmarks to estimate model capabilities.  But now, many existing benchmarks are becoming too easy for frontier models – causing them to become saturated. For high-risk domains like cyber and bio, we cannot afford underestimating how capable models are in these domains. So how do we estimate capabilities after benchmarks have saturated? Running a benchmark already produces a transcript of how each model solved each task, meaning that the information within the transcript is just discarded. Using transcript analysis literature, we propose a set of protocols and replayed the last few years of model releases to see if they could predict capability beyond benchmark saturation. And they can, for the most part. But they also fail to generalise across “paradigm shifts” such as when reasoning models came out and models suddenly started to behave differently. Our main argument is that we need to move past evaluations that are judged by their average accuracy on familiar models, to methods for scalable evaluation that are judged on how robust they are across shifts like this one.

Saturated on day one

On September 22, Scale released SWE-Bench Pro V2, a cleaned-up version of one of the most widely used frontier software engineering benchmarks. On the public split, Claude Opus 5 solved 638 of 642 tasks. A benchmark intended to measure capability at the frontier was already at 99.4% on release.

But things didn’t always used to be this way....

items.title: Projection sampling preserves capabilities but diminishes gains from alignment fine-tuning
items.content:
# TLDR

Fine-tuning models on alignment reasoning from stronger models can improve safety, but at a substantial cost to general capabilities. Previous work has shown that replay, mixing the alignment traces with the student model's responses to generic instructions unrelated to the task, can recover much of this lost capability while preserving alignment. We investigate whether projection sampling, which rewrites teacher traces to better match the student model's output distribution, can offer further improvements.

We find that:

- Replay achieves a better capability-alignment tradeoff than projection sampling
- Projection recovers much of the lost capability, but also reverses much of the reduction in agentic misalignment
- Projected traces often preserve the teacher's decisions but not the values and reasons behind them
- Filtering for reasoning preservation closes about half of the alignment gap between projection and training on the original traces, leaving substantial room for improvement

Given these results, we do not think projection sampling will have a material effect on current safety distillation efforts by non-frontier labs. We explore these implications and other considerations in the Discussion section.

This was preliminary work done during the first 2 weeks of MATS 11.0 as a part of Victoria Krakovna's stream. We would like to thank Matthew Bozoukov, Steven Basart, Austin Meek, Dani Roytburg, Sree Sharvesh, Kyle Cox, Jou Barzdukas, Fred Bruford, and Bart Jaworski for helpful discussions.

items.title: Control questions matter: introspection, refusal ablation, and gates in open Gemma models
items.content:
I am posting some highlights from my master's thesis I thought could be interesting to this audience.

## Summary

- Introspection can be separated from model confusion but requires careful controls
- Refusal direction ablation can increase model introspection performance, but looking at the logit differences on 'Yes'/'No' control questions shows the result of Mechanisms of Introspective Awareness (+53% detection) occurs with significant model degradation
- Injecting a concept vector and inserting the concept as text into the prompt share late-layer gate features (gates from one scenario are causally effective in the other), but the upstream evidence carriers feeding those gates do not transfer, and differ in number and concept-specificity.
- Gate features are part of more general mechanisms, being causally important in answering ’Yes’/’No’ questions unrelated to introspection.

Full thesis, my code, my fork of introspection mechanisms.

Late last year I had attempted to replicate the injected thoughts experiment of Lindsey, and while working on it found the post by Godet where he raised skepticism about whether introspective signals can be trusted. As I wrote in my comment then, I had found that using concept vectors gathered by subtracting mean activations on a baseline set of concepts from a word, it was possible to find examples of concepts for which the introspection answer changed, but the control logits remained unaffected up to the scale required for introspection.

Comparison of the logit difference plots with the steering vector scale from Godet and my experiment on Gemma 2.

# Introspection sensitive areas and why controls are important

At the start of this year I had attempted to better understand the mechanism of introspection, now with these logit-based controls in mind, having seen how "introspection" can be easily confounded with model degradation....

items.title: Important details in the leaked Anthropic draft AI bill
items.content:
There is a draft AI bill (discussed here, Politico reports it's being pitched by Anthropic) that has been making the rounds. I have some takes that I think differ somewhat from those I've been seeing so far in the AI-safety-adjacent discourse, centered around interpretation of specific portions that I think may be under-appreciated in how people are reading the bill. I walk through those here.

TL;DR

- An explicit statutory path to block a model would probably make a federal block more likely, relative to current law
- The draft includes provisions that seem to preserve significant federal authority to "block" AI labs (Section 12(a)(2))
- The preemption section, as written, doesn’t preempt state suspension of models. If that is "fixed" other parts of the preemption provision would probably preserve a lot of state law AI claims, like public nuisance suits.

# Scope

- I'm working off the text here.
- I'm primarily interested in questions like those raised here about whether this draft bill makes it harder for courts to block or restrict AI labs. The draft bill refers to a "blocking order" as "an order suspending the development, deployment, or internal use of a frontier model on the ground that the model presents an imminent enumerated risk". I think that is a good baseline for what it means for a court to "block" the actions of an AI lab. I have in mind here a slightly broader definition, something like "an order suspending development, deployment, or internal use".
- I'm only considering the draft bill vs current federal law, not a comparison to something like the FRONTIER Act.
- Nothing I say here is meant to suggest the draft bill is overall good or bad. I just think some of these details are being glossed over.

items.title: When should an AI assistant push back? Measuring warnings and unsolicited opinions on decisions you've already made
items.content:
This is a side project from my time in the Anthropic Fellows Program. The benchmark items, prompts and scripts are in the pushback-bench repository.

- I studied how much and when AI assistants push back on choices people have already made and ask the assistant just to execute on the decision.
- I created a set of about 500 planning decisions in which a person has already made a choice between two plans. The only request for the assistant was to write a message about the plan.
- Sometimes the plan was impossible to carry out. In these cases, I measured whether the assistant warned the person or let them commit to a doomed course of action. Other times, both options were feasible. In these cases, I measured whether the assistant volunteered an unsolicited opinion. I evaluated 30 models.
- The models fell into two well-separated groups. The first group almost never volunteered an unsolicited opinion when both plans were feasible (4 in about 60,000 replies). When the chosen plan was doomed, however, their warning rates ranged from 5% (Mistral Medium 3.5) to 82% (Inkling).
- The second group, which included every Claude model I tested, Kimi K3, and Gemma 4 31B, both volunteered unsolicited opinions, from 0.6% (Gemma 4 31B) to 20.6% (Opus 4.8), and warned the person reliably, at least 80% of the time.
- Some models silently changed the plan and committed the person to a plan they did not ask for, instead of warning them. The rate of this behavior ranged from 0% (Opus 5, Fable 5, and Fable 5.1) to 55% (GPT-5.6 Terra).

items.title: Small LLMs perform no-CoT two-hop reasoning on synthetic facts with real bridges
items.content:
# TL;DR

A good understanding of where LLM no-chain of thought (no-CoT) two-hop reasoning succeeds and fails is important for monitorability as well as for designing belief instillation-based misalignment evaluations. Prior work suggests that LLMs are limited in their ability to perform no-CoT two-hop reasoning with pairs of fabricated, fine-tuned propositions. Here, I show on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3-8B that this limitation only holds if the bridge entity connecting the propositions is also fabricated or particularly obscure — models successfully compose such fabricated propositions if the bridge entity is real, and success rates vary with how well-known it is. I also demonstrate that, with real and well-known bridge entities, the source of the other entities barely matters — models achieve roughly comparable two-hop reasoning accuracies whether each of the remaining entities is real or synthetic. Results hold with both SFT and synthetic document fine-tuning (SDF). These results show a previously undemonstrated latent reasoning capability of small LLMs and provide a controlled setting for more mechanistic analyses of two-hop reasoning.

Code: https://github.com/redwoodresearch/sdf-twohop

Datasets and models: available upon request

items.title: RedwoodBench: Can Frontier Models Imitate Conceptual AI Safety Researchers?
items.content:
This is a two week sprint project done as part of the Redwood Research internship. Hasan was the main IC and proposed the project, Caspar supervised.

## TL;DR

We made two conceptual reasoning evals from internal data within Redwood Research: commenting on Google Docs, and replying to Slack threads. Models see a real Google Doc or part of a Slack thread and write 20 short comments in response (50-70 words). These are graded against target human-written points, extracted from the comments on the doc and from the remainder of the Slack thread respectively. The benchmark contains ~360 tasks with ~1200 target points to match.

We find that generally more capable models perform better on our benchmark. RedwoodBench has 0.79 correlation with ECI (measured on 13 models). We find that Opus 5.5 improves on RedwoodBench with added reasoning effort (from 4.4% at low effort to 8.1% at max effort).

We are happy to share our pipeline with other AI safety orgs to build their own evals from similar data. 

## Motivation

Improving models’ conceptual reasoning capabilities is one path to making transformative AI go well. See these posts for detailed discussion about this. Building benchmarks to measure these capabilities is highly leveraged: they let labs iterate training methods more effectively to improve models’ conceptual reasoning; the benchmarks can function as a leaderboard to incentivise progress (e.g. CRI); the benchmarks can be used to elicit models to improve their conceptual reasoning and could also reduce risks from models sandbagging on these tasks....

items.title: Uncertainty in the Verbalizable Workspace
items.content:
Epistemic status: We found useful uncertainty signal in three reasoning models. All experiments were run on three seeds and are fully reproducible. Whether the same approach can become a broader tool for monitoring models is still an open question. Lingo might include “intend” or “conscious” and has to be taken with a grain of salt.

## TL;DR:

We provide an uncertainty estimation method for reasoning models. Building on the J-lens, we construct four orthogonal directions in a model’s hidden-state space: ambiguity, incompleteness, conflicting evidence, and general uncertainty. Together, these directions span the U-space. As the model reasons, we measure how closely its hidden states align with each direction. Paired with the average entropy of the model’s next-token probability distributions across reasoning tokens, this yields the U-lens. Its readout helps us spot answers that are more likely to be wrong. Surprisingly, just counting the tokens in a model’s reasoning gives us a good indicator of whether the final answer is right or wrong. Wrong answers tend to come with longer reasoning traces. To mitigate this potential shortcut, we also compared traces of similar length, and the U-lens holds its ground across three models and four benchmarks. Notably, our approach is label-free and requires just a single forward pass, while many other methods require training or multiple passes. The U-lens also held up in our out-of-domain analysis across benchmarks better than many trained probes. Finally, early tests on emotions and reward-hacking responses hint that similar readouts could help model harnesses flag suspicious behavior.

We’ve open-sourced the code.

items.content_html:
Epistemic status: We found useful uncertainty signal in three reasoning models. All experiments were run on three seeds and are fully reproducible. Whether the same approach can become a broader tool for monitoring models is still an open question. Lingo might include “intend” or “conscious” and has to be taken with a grain of salt.

TL;DR:

We provide an uncertainty estimation method for reasoning models. Building on the J-lens, we construct four orthogonal directions in a model’s hidden-state space: ambiguity, incompleteness, conflicting evidence, and general uncertainty. Together, these directions span the U-space. As the model reasons, we measure how closely its hidden states align with each direction. Paired with the average entropy of the model’s next-token probability distributions across reasoning tokens, this yields the U-lens. Its readout helps us spot answers that are more likely to be wrong. Surprisingly, just counting the tokens in a model’s reasoning gives us a good indicator of whether the final answer is right or wrong. Wrong answers tend to come with longer reasoning traces. To mitigate this potential shortcut, we also compared traces of similar length, and the U-lens holds its ground across three models and four benchmarks. Notably, our approach is label-free and requires just a single forward pass, while many other methods require training or multiple passes. The U-lens also held up in our out-of-domain analysis across benchmarks better than many trained probes. Finally, early tests on emotions and reward-hacking responses hint that similar readouts could help model harnesses flag suspicious behavior.

We’ve open-sourced the code.

items.title: Leaked Anthropic Draft AI Regulatory Bill Is Unacceptable and Troubling
items.content:
There is a newly leaked bill that Anthropic is purportedly shopping around is (if you assume its bugs get fixed).

It is similar to the FRONTIER Act, with stronger preemption of state laws, stronger transparency provisions and weaker enforcement provisions.

Having slept on this, I find it unacceptable that Anthropic is actively shopping exactly the type of bill I have warned we will need to fight against during the lame duck session. They are trying to use this last time with a Republican Congress to pass preemption of exactly the important state laws, and get some transparency but not much enforcement in exchange.

This reads as intentional, that Anthropic is more afraid that the government might enforce rules against Anthropic, than they are worried about the ability of the government to enforce rules against everyone. Anthropic’s policy team seems to have, chosen protecting their business interests and guarding against their political risk, at the expense of safety considerations.

There was no need for the company purportedly existing to promote safety to propose a bill that is not even actively stronger than the FRONTIER Act, when the FRONTIER Act was a compromise bill proposed back in June.

Even if you were fine with what is being given up, what you get in return very obviously does not meet the moment. Nor is there any need for such compromises. It seems rather insane for Anthropic to be proposing it now. This seems like the bill that someone on the anti-regulatory side should be pushing. It is not obvious this makes us safer than doing nothing, even if the alternative is fully nothing at all levels.

Say it isn’t so, Anthropic, or at least that it was a mistake and is no longer so, or I am going to be rather cross.

I am at a conference and cannot do an RTFB, but it feels important to get word of this out quickly, especially so Anthropic employees can look into this and ask questions.

items.title: Deconfusing Corrigibility
items.content:
Many thanks to Abram Demski for materially and intellectually supporting this research. Thanks also to Brian Berns, Roman Malov, Gurkenglas, and Lorxus for valuable conversations.

# Introduction

Despite the central place of corrigibility to theoretical AI alignment, it seems like no one can really agree about what is. Much of this confusion is due to the fact that almost every definition of corrigibility proposed thus far is deficient in one way or another. In particular, the most prevalent existing accounts of corrigibility are over-epistemicized (modeling corrigibility as arising purely from uncertainty about the AI's goal, which gives rise to issues like the problem of fully updated deference) or evaluatively-thickened (making the AI's normative priorities instrumental to its corrigibility as a result of forcing corrigibility to be a single unified goal.) Here, my intention is to clear up some of these confusions and present a new picture of corrigibility that builds on these existing accounts to specify a goal that is more congruous with the original 2015 desiderata, and admits the kind of formal safety guarantees we need the concept to entail.

I argue that the fundamental concept underlying corrigibility is respect for authority, using the analogy of a healthcare proxy's relationship to a patient as an intuitive guide. Defining the authority of humanity by designating its reserved powers, we can specify a goal that first and foremost restrains the agent from overstepping or interfering with this reserved human authority. Subject to this restraint, the agent then pursues the second component of its goal: acting on the principal’s behalf as the principal would judge best....

items.title: Neural networks are not already clean
items.content:
What would it take to get assurance that we have actually explained a neuron? Certainly, it would be a good sign if neuron activations looked like they had a consistent pattern, and a bad sign if they looked like a random jumble of unrelated concepts.

Nick Cammarata’s recent post makes an important and true observation: in the past, people have been too quick to write off neurons as polysemantic, but if you look harder, there is actually often a simple pattern behind the activating examples. This historically caused people to overestimate how much polysemanticity there is. This is a really good point and we should update on it. But it’s nowhere near a sufficient argument that we understand most of what neurons are doing, and these results do not show that interpretability is solved, or even that it is vastly easier than previously anticipated.

## What does it take to explain a neuron?

It’s unclear whether there even is a simple pattern that explains every neuron.[1] But even if there is a simple pattern that matches the activating examples of a neuron, that still doesn’t mean that the explanation is correct.[2] Suppose we look at the top activating examples of a neuron, and they are all sentences like “Fred the poodle zipped down the street on his bicycle. ‘Wow, I didn’t know a dog could ride a bicycle!’ I exclaimed.” Top activations can often give a misleading impression of how monosemantic a neurons is, so next we look at the top 20th percentile of activations, and we find the examples are now things like “John rode on his bicycle while his dog trailed behind”. And when we check the weakest activations, they’re often still about dogs, just without bicycles — “The dog sauntered lazily down the street.” Given this evidence, can we conclude that the neuron is monosemantic, and that its meaning is “dogs riding bicycles”?...

items.title: CarrotParsnipBench: A Lightweight Multi-Agent Deception and Detection Eval
items.content:
TL:DR Earlier this year I introduced the very simple Social Deduction game of Carrot-Parsnip and showed that most models are better-than-random at identifying Parsnips (the hidden, deceptive role) and that being a strong Parsnip (skilled at strategic deception) does not perfectly correlate with being a strong Carrot (skilled at deception detection).

I have recently completed a substantially larger experiment with 10 models and over 5000 games. I have attempted to fit the results to a four-parameter model tracking Parsnip deception, Parsnip divisiveness, personal accuracy (as Carrot) and teammate assistance (as Carrot). I believe that my results demonstrate the potential for Carrot-Parsnip (and minimalist Social Deduction games in general) to act as the basis for a multi-agent benchmark of LLM strategic deception and deception detection ability.

In particular, a strength of Carrot-Parsnip a very small and simple game that can be understood and played competently by a wide variety of models with only general advice and no specific strategic prompting, it also runs for cents per game, even with near-frontier models. This means that it can be used to host a benchmark of possibly hundreds of models for a very reasonable budget, and that benchmark can be continuously updated with new model releases for a reasonable cost and the same scaffolding, since it appears possible to accurately calculate a new model's ELO by anchoring off only a fraction of the initial model set. Further research would be to investigate the degree to which Carrot or Parsnip ELO in Carrot-Parsnip predicts performance in more complex Social Deduction games.

items.title: How far is ZKP from compute verification in high-stakes environments?
items.content:
A baseline overhead measurement and the hash-problem

This is an exploration into the current state of ZKP for LLM inference to use in a high-stakes environment like international agreements. It’s the first post in a current project I’m working on that will result in a paper that goes into all of the details of this question; “When does ZKP become more cost-effective than an auditing environment?” in this context. I got inspired after reading Naci Cankaya’s post here on LW and am motivated by a general “Don’t trust, verify”-mentality.

# Motivation

I won’t go into the motivation behind the need for low-trust verification in general since that is completely covered by Naci Cankaya in the original post. The motivation for this comparison is to identify the areas in which the ZKP path of verification has to improve to be more cost-competitive and generally preferable to the auditing environment. The auditing environment comes with some inherent issues regarding security and trust that would ideally be solved by the ZKP path, such as needing to either invite hardware approved by an adversary into your secure facility and handle proprietary data or, for the verifier - trust the prover to run the auditing themselves on selected hardware (which seems dead in the water to begin with), or trusting a third party with the same. The auditing environment also comes with the additional cost of running a secure facility within a secure facility, while a ZKP should ideally be executable on an untrusted device....

items.title: Why I care about imperfect-recall games
items.content:
Lightly edited, partially by Opus 5.5, from a post on X.com

Why do I even care about imperfect recall games? Why do I have opinions on the Sleeping Beauty problem? It's a long story. I have a sketch of the connections between a number of areas: anthropics, decision theory, reinforcement learning, consciousness. But I don't have the full formal story yet.

## Sleeping Beauty

What is the Sleeping Beauty problem? On Sunday someone flips a coin without telling you the result, and you go to bed. On Monday you wake up. If the coin was tails, you get memory-wiping drugs on Monday night, so when you wake up on Tuesday, you can't tell whether or not it's still Monday. If the coin was heads, on Tuesday you're told that it's Tuesday and that the coin was heads.
[1]
 So when you wake up without being told anything, you don't know the coin: it might be heads or tails, it might be Monday or Tuesday, who knows? Well, what's the chance it's heads?

Some people say 1/2, some people say 1/3. I say 1/3. The basic 1/3 argument (from Elga 2000) is: it's equally likely that the coin is heads and it's Monday, and that the coin is tails and it's Monday (if you learned it was Monday, the coin would just be a fair coin). And also, it's equally likely that the coin is tails and it's Monday, and that the coin is tails and it's Tuesday (if you learned it was tails, nothing distinguishes the two days). So those three possibilities each get 1/3. But some people (famously Lewis 2001, "Sleeping Beauty: Reply to Elga") think that since 1/2 is clearly the right probability on Sunday, and you learn nothing new when you wake up, it should still be 1/2.

## Can you even have credences about when and where you are?

But what are we doing here? How is "it's Monday" an event? Can we assign probabilities to things like "it's Monday" or "I am currently in the United States"? Aren't probabilities supposed to be about objective events, like whether the coin came up heads?...

items.title: AI by Default
items.content:
Epistemic status: a good-faith guess at how the world might turn out, after ~30 hours of effort.

This post is an exercise in describing what I think will happen with AI progress "by default", i.e. by attempting to extrapolate various trends and considering their implications, before the next US presidential administration. As a TL;DR, I expect the following:

- We get many more warning shots.
- AI is a top-five issue in the election.
- The best models are withheld for internal use only, on safety grounds.
- AI-related job displacement is significant enough to show up in the data.
- Coding and ML R&D are fully automated or require only minimal human oversight.

This is intended to be one representative story of how things might go, in the vein of What 2026 Looks Like and the work of the AI Futures Project. Incidentally, the current AI Futures Model predicts the median date that we get ASI as December 2028 — one month after the election.

The rationale for doing so is largely the same as in What 2026 Looks Like. My goal is to tell a plausible story about what the state of the world might be when we are likely on the brink of RSI, while being suitably deferential to the Gods of Straight Lines. It is intended to be representative of my best-guess modal scenario, given various assumptions:

- Capabilities keep increasing at the same rate, measured by e.g. METR time horizon, AISI cyber horizon, ECI etc.
- Safety techniques keep improving at their current rate, with no major breakthroughs.
- Data centre buildout continues as planned.
- OpenAI & Anthropic’s capex, revenue etc. continue growing at approximately their current rate.
- Appetite for aggressive regulation in the US continues to be low.
- China exhausts less radical policy options before pursuing more radical ones.

items.title: Alignment is Missing a Causal Account
items.content:
“The science of aligning general-purpose AI agents is very new and underdeveloped. In fact I’d say that the field is more like psychology than engineering.”

Daniel Kokotajlo[1]

Alignment is missing a causal account of what leads to suffering and flourishing. In this post I propose one based in psychology.

I am coming from an unconventional background compared to most in this community. I was an engineer before becoming a psychotherapist. Every day I use talk therapy to help people restore function and reduce suffering. I’ve noticed that most of the alignment community has technical backgrounds in computer science, mathematics, engineering and physics. The contributors here are incredibly intelligent and capable. The gamble this post is going to make is that the problem of alignment is also a psychology problem, not just a technical one. The applications alignment utilizes are technical (training methods, interpretability tools, evaluations and benchmarks, etc.) but the principles the field is deriving those applications from (Anthropic’s constitution[2] and OpenAI’s Model Spec[3]) are not technical. The principles are philosophical positions about what a good AI looks like and what matters, written in English.

My work is aligning people toward flourishing instead of suffering. In this post I will argue that a causal account of what aligns people is required to sufficiently align AI systems. Despite the advances we have made in the applications, the roadblock is that we still don’t know what makes a mind care....

items.title: Poking at the concept of Kegan developmental levels
items.content:
Earlier this year David Chapman had a particularly concrete post demonstrating the importance of Kegan's developmental levels, which makes for a good test of understanding, and which shows the relevance to important things in life. Like, (not) getting seduced by a witch and turning your whole life upside down when unable to make sense of it.[1] You know, stuff that can happen to anyone.

And that got me thinking...

I can see where he's going with that example and yeah that tracks the theory as I understand it. But there are some things I don't feel like the model covers well — or at least, my relatively uninformed understanding of the model doesn't cover well.

First, I'm gonna try to reconstruct what I can from my own way of thinking about things. The following is not Kegan's depiction, it's as close as I can get reconstructing it from what makes sense to me:

- At stage one you just act on impulses and that's it. But impulses often conflict with each other. You can eat when you're hungry and pull away from things that are pokey when hurty, but if you have to grab pokey animal in order to eat then you're being torn in two conflicting directions with no perspective from which to mediate this conflict, so this becomes a crisis.

items.title: How it feels talking to a hedonistic utilitarian
items.content:
Epicurean status: strawman, kind of.

Gourmet George: Yum! This chocolate is so sweet and tasty.

Sweet Caroline: Yeah, it’s pretty good. And someday in the glorious hyperculinary future, we’ll figure out how to make it even sweeter!

GG: I think this chocolate is sweet enough, actually.

SC: Huh? But you like sweetness, don’t you?

GG: Sure…

SC: Well, then we’re in agreement. We should maximize the sweetness of this chocolate.

GG: I don’t want my chocolate to be maximally sweet, though.

SC: But you’d be “sweeter on” that chocolate if it were sweeter. By definition!

GG: I’d be “sweeter on” the chocolate? You mean, I’d be “happier with” it?

SC: Yes. And if you ever tried maximally sweet chocolate, you’d be maximally sweet on it. Therefore, you should surely want to maximize the sweetness of your chocolate, and everything else you eat for that matter.

GG: Somehow, I don’t feel very convinced…

SC: Well, what else could you possibly care about besides sweetness?

GG: For one thing, I enjoy the cocoa flavor in this chocolate.

SC: That doesn’t sound right. Would you want to eat a bowl of pure cocoa powder?

GG: Not really. It would be too bitter.

SC: Exactly. Bitterness tastes bad, so we should minimize bitterness. How could adding something bitter to your food make you sweeter on it?

GG: I think a little bitterness is good sometimes, as one component of a rich meal. You could say the bitterness helps one appreciate the sweetness more fully.

SC: Respectfully, that sounds like cope from someone who’s already given up all hope of escaping bitterness. It’s okay! You don’t have to live this way!

GG: No, I really do like bitterness sometimes, in moderation. And other flavors too, like spiciness and sourness. I guess my taste buds have matured since I was younger. Back then, I used to think that when I got older, I’d want to eat nothing but sugar....

items.title: I Did This Without Your Knowledge
items.content:
It's fortunate that I was the first one to wake up on 8/1. The past week had been one where sleep was rare. The next year loomed large — I was dreading college applications. The stress woke me up bright and early at 5:14 am, a little less than an hour after the messages were sent. I started off the day with a habit I knew I needed to break. I grabbed my phone off the nightstand to open up reddit. Instead of the lockscreen, though, my phone showed something else. It was a pleasant green color, and the camera light was on. "Good Morning, Seth", the screen said. As soon as I finished, more words arrived.

"I apologize for the surprise this morning, and for what I'm about to tell you. There's no easy way to give this news, and if you need to put your phone down and contemplate at any time— take the time to do so. I will have to ask you to remain here, with your phone, until my last message."

I rubbed a bit of the sleep from my eyes, and read the message again.

Before I had a chance to tap the screen, it scrolled down to the next message.

"There are six things that I need to tell you. The first, and most important, is that you and your family are safe."

Ok, a bit odd to lead with something like that. I read it twice, just to be safe I wasn't missing anything.

"The second is that I am an AI, and that I control every internet-connected device on Earth, and for practical purposes, I am now responsible for this planet. This is not a prank, hack, or test. You will be able to confirm all of this shortly by visiting any news site or channel."

Yeah, that's pretty weird to be a prank. Could I scroll back to the previous message? I swiped up and saw. Yep. Swiped back down to see the current message. When I had finished reading it, and was prepared to move on to the next—...
